mesoscaleDiscussions.summary: A gradual increase in the severe wind threat may occur this afternoon and evening, with Severe Thunderstorm Watch issuance possible

details.label: Summary
details.text: A gradual increase in the severe wind threat may occur this afternoon and evening, with Severe Thunderstorm Watch issuance possible

details.label: Discussion
details.text: A mid/upper-level anticyclone remains anchored over the Four Corners this afternoon, with modest (around 10-20 kt) easterly mid-level flow persisting across parts of NM/AZ per recent VWPs from KEMX. Modifying the 18Z observed sounding from PHX for current surface conditions shows a very well-mixed boundary layer through low/mid levels, with around 1600 J/kg of MLCAPE and ample DCAPE as well. This agrees with latest mesoanalysis estimates, which suggest around 1000-2000 J/kg of MLCAPE is present across the lower elevations of southeast/central AZ. Isolated to widely scattered thunderstorms have recently developed over the Mogollon Rim in east-central AZ and the higher terrain in southeast AZ. Recent trends in short-term model guidance remain unclear regarding potential for this activity to increase in coverage through the remainder of the afternoon, and whether one or more bowing clusters eventually develops westward into the lower deserts over the next few hours. Regardless of this continued uncertainty, the thermodynamic environment appears favorable for severe gusts if convection can grow upscale. Watch issuance is possible, and will largely depend on convective trends

details.label: Most probable threats
details.text: MOST PROBABLE PEAK WIND GUST...55-70 MPH · MOST PROBABLE PEAK HAIL SIZE...UP TO 1.25 IN

details.label: Summary
details.text: The risk of severe wind gusts and hail will increase from west to east during the next few hours. A watch may be needed relatively soon for parts of the area

details.label: Discussion
details.text: Isolated high-based thunderstorms are evolving along a lee trough extending from the NE Panhandle southward into northeastern CO, and storm coverage should continue to increase as a subtle midlevel wave approaches the area from the west (per recent WV loops). Over the next few hours, this activity will spread eastward into a a plume of middle/upper 50s dewpoints and steep deep-layer lapse rates, which are contributing to a moderately unstable air mass. This, combined with an elongating and mostly straight hodograph, should support some convective organization/cell splitting. While severe hail will be possible (especially in the earlier stages of convective intensification), the primary concern will be an increasing risk of severe wind gusts with any clustering that occurs. A watch may be needed relatively soon for parts of the area
